item.itunes:title: I stopped using CCleaner after finding a free open-source cleaner that finds more junk
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a long time, CCleaner was one of those third-party tools I'd install on my PC without a second thought. Since I literally grew up with this software, I never felt the need to look for an alternative. Even when its reputation hit rock bottom by 2020, I continued using it out of habit, mostly because I was so familiar with it. I've seen so many people recommend BleachBit since then, but I never bothered giving it a try until recently.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I decided to ditch CCleaner partly because of all the controversies in recent years, but also because I was getting tired of the upgrade prompts. Since BleachBit is completely free and open-source, I knew I wouldn't have to deal with any of that, which is what made it appealing at first. And after trying it out, I can confidently say that it offers way more than I expected. All I wanted was a cleaner that covered the basics, but BleachBit showed me how much junk I'd been overlooking over years of using CCleaner.

I disabled this Windows 11 feature and instantly reclaimed almost 25GB of storage

I'd rather use that 25GB for an indie game.

5
By  Hamlin Rozario

BleachBit looks in places I never thought to clean

Deep Scan targets certain file types that regular cleaning might overlook

Just like any third-party cleaner, CCleaner can get rid of the usual Windows junk, browser data, and leftovers from apps that accumulate over time. In fact, it now even lets you clean files from AI tools. BleachBit, on the other hand, takes a slightly different approach to finding unnecessary files. Of course, you can still use it to clean normally, but its Deep Scan feature is what helps you find more junk. It looks for specific file types that might be scattered across your PC. These could be backup files, temporary files, and Thumbs.db files, or even developer-related folders like node_modules.

By default, BleachBit prevents you from cleaning anything under Deep Scan unless you enable Expert mode from its Preferences menu. This makes sense because you don't want to accidentally delete your backup files or any other data you might still need. I highly recommend using the Preview feature before actually cleaning anything since it shows you exactly which files will be removed and how much space you could potentially free up. All in all, I'd treat Deep Scan results as something to inspect, not a list of files that need to be deleted just because BleachBit found them.

You're not limited to its default cleaning options

Winapp2.ini adds thousands of community-driven cleaners

When you open BleachBit for the first time and scroll through the sidebar, you're not going to be particularly impressed with the number of cleaning options it has to offer. But the good news is that it supports the Winapp2.ini database, which actually has its roots in the CCleaner community. You can use it to add so many more cleaners than the ones already included. You just need to go to Preferences -> Updates, check the box next to Download and update cleaners from community (winapp2.ini), and restart BleachBit. You might have to restart it a second time if the additional cleaners don't appear right away, though.

After I did this, I saw many cleaners in the sidebar that weren't there before, including ones for Adobe software, game installers, and even PowerToys. There's even a separate Utilities category now, which lists cleaning options for third-party tools like CrystalDiskInfo, MSI Afterburner, and even CCleaner itself. Sure, I probably won't use half of these cleaning options, but I still like that I can extend the cleaner without waiting for developers to add support for every app I use.

CCleaner technically has more going for it

But it's mostly just more of what I don't need

At the end of the day, CCleaner isn't just a cleaner, even though the name suggests otherwise. If anything, it's more of an all-in-one PC maintenance utility and comes with several features you won't find in BleachBit. For instance, I've relied on its uninstaller for years, but these days I just use Windows 11's Settings app. Then, there's Duplicate Finder, which lets you scan for identical files taking up space. You also get a Startup Manager to control which apps launch with Windows. And let's not forget it can clean your registry, which has been a topic of debate for as long as I can remember.

I could keep going about Performance Optimizer, Software Updater, and Driver Updater, but those are mostly locked behind a paywall. CCleaner is feature-packed, but aside from its uninstaller, I've mostly used it to clean temporary files, browser caches, and other junk on my PC. So, if a completely free app can take over and find even more junk, I don't see why I should keep putting up with CCleaner anymore. Sure, BleachBit's UI isn't fancy, but it's not like I'm cleaning my PC every week for that to matter.

Looking back, I should've ditched CCleaner years ago

I probably should've looked for alternatives when CCleaner's reputation started taking a hit, but I guess I was just too used to it to bother with anything else. Now that I've tried BleachBit, though, I get what the hype is all about. It has helped me find junk I never even thought to look for with CCleaner, and that's before considering all the community-driven cleaners it supports. And the fact that I get all of this for free without having to put up with upgrade prompts is reason enough to move on from CCleaner altogether.

item.title: I replaced Google Maps with this open-source alternative and I barely miss it
item.itunes:title: I replaced Google Maps with this open-source alternative and I barely miss it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You've probably heard people say that even if they've ditched most of Google's apps, there's one they just can't seem to give up: Google Maps. Interestingly, despite relying heavily on Google's ecosystem, from its Workspace apps to some of the experimental tools coming out of Google Labs, Google Maps was one app I barely ever opened.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

There were two reasons for that. I don't drive, and I don't live in a particularly walkable city. I rarely step out of the house to go somewhere I don't already know the directions to, and when I do, I'm usually with a friend who drives. But I've been traveling quite a bit lately, and Google Maps has gone from an app I'd rarely open to one of the most-used apps on my phone.

While I've grown to appreciate just how useful Google Maps is, I've also started wondering whether I really need to rely on Google to get around. So, I decided to put that to the test by replacing it with CoMaps, a completely free and open-source alternative.

CoMaps is a completely open-source alternative to Google Maps

A familiar app with a different philosophy

Now, this isn't my first time trying open-source Google Maps alternatives. I've been experimenting with them for a while now, and I even wrote about three alternatives I tested just a few days ago. One of the tools I covered was Organic Maps, a fairly well-known open-source Google Maps alternative. It's long been known for its privacy-focused approach and is built on OpenStreetMap data.

Interestingly, CoMaps is actually a fork of Organic Maps. It emerged in May 2025 following disagreements between Organic Maps' contributors and shareholders over the project's governance, financial transparency, and future direction. Several contributors ultimately decided to branch off and create CoMaps, a community-driven, not-for-profit alternative that prioritizes transparency and open-source development.

This means the two apps have a fair bit in common. Like Organic Maps, CoMaps prioritizes user privacy, doesn't require an account, and lets you download maps for offline navigation. It supports walking, cycling, and driving directions. It also doesn't bombard you with ads and is completely free from AI features you never asked for.

CoMaps takes its community-led approach seriously

A little help from the crowd goes a long way

CoMaps is built by its community for its community, and it seems to take this philosophy very seriously. Since it relies on OpenStreetMap data, users can contribute to the maps themselves, whether that's adding a missing business, correcting outdated opening hours, or updating information about an existing location. You can even make some of these changes directly through the app, although you'll need an OpenStreetMap account to do so.

While you can do all of the above with Organic Maps too, CoMaps takes things a step further with its integration with Mangrove Reviews. One of my biggest frustrations with the open-source alternatives I previously tested was the lack of ratings and reviews. After all, when you're exploring an unfamiliar city, knowing how to get somewhere is only half the battle. You also need to figure out whether that restaurant or café is actually worth visiting.

CoMaps attempts to address this with community-powered reviews. Since August 2026, Android users have been able to see star ratings and written reviews for places through Mangrove, an independent, open review platform. While you can technically access Mangrove reviews separately when using Organic Maps, CoMaps integrates them directly into the app, so you don't have to switch between services. Interestingly, these reviews are also downloaded alongside the maps, meaning you can access them even when you're offline. You can also contribute your own reviews through external tools like MapComplete.

There's a catch, though. Mangrove's database is still nowhere near as extensive as Google's. As of October 2026, it has just over 10,000 reviews worldwide, compared to the millions available on larger platforms. This means finding reviews for places near you can be a challenge. Still, it's an interesting step toward addressing one of the biggest advantages Google Maps has over its open-source competitors.

CoMaps has offline maps that actually work offline

Google Maps can't walk the walk

One of my biggest frustrations with Google Maps is just how limited its offline maps are. I mean, what good are offline maps if they can't actually give you the directions you need when you're offline? Plus, what's worse than discovering that limitation when you've already lost internet access?

I learned this the hard way when I was in Berlin for IFA. I needed to get a local SIM card from a store in the city center, which was closing in about an hour. I was alone in an unfamiliar city, had no mobile data, and needed to figure out how to get there as quickly as possible.

Now, you'd think having downloaded Google Maps' offline maps beforehand would've been enough. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case. While I could see the streets around me, Google Maps couldn't give me walking directions. With time running out, I ended up having to ask strangers for directions along the way.

The problem is that Google Maps only supports driving directions when you're offline. Walking, cycling, and public transit directions all require an internet connection. Given that I don't drive and spend most of my time walking whenever I'm traveling, this is a pretty major inconvenience.

This is where CoMaps makes a massive difference. Like Google Maps, you can download maps of entire regions beforehand. But unlike Google's offering, CoMaps lets you search for places, plan walking routes, and get turn-by-turn directions even when you're completely offline. You also get voice-guided navigation, and since GPS doesn't require an internet connection, you can still track your location without mobile data.

Essentially, instead of simply having a downloaded map that shows you where you are, you have an actual navigation app that can help you get to where you need to go.

The biggest thing I'm missing out on is live traffic data

Luckily, that's not my biggest concern

If there's one thing Google Maps is undeniably good at, it's live traffic data. Thanks to its massive user base, Google Maps can provide real-time traffic updates, identify congestion, and suggest alternative routes to help you avoid getting stuck in traffic. It's one of those features that can make a massive difference when you're trying to get somewhere on time.

Unfortunately, this is also one of the biggest things CoMaps lacks. It doesn't offer real-time traffic information, meaning you won't know whether a particular road is congested or if there's a faster route available. That said, this isn't much of a dealbreaker for me. I don't drive, and when I'm traveling, I'm almost always exploring on foot. So, while I can certainly see why the lack of live traffic data might be a major drawback for some people, it's not a feature I personally rely on very often.

I stopped using Android Auto's navigation and switched to offline maps, and now I never worry about signal loss

No signal, no problem

4
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The good news is that CoMaps' developers are actively working on bringing live traffic information to the app. According to its official documentation, the team has already started developing its own traffic data server, with the goal of using open, privacy-preserving data sources. There's no confirmed timeline for when the feature will arrive, but it's reassuring to know that the developers are working on addressing this limitation.

Google Maps does more, but CoMaps does enough

Ultimately, I don't think CoMaps is going to replace Google Maps for everyone. Google still has the upper hand when it comes to live traffic information, its massive database of reviews, and the sheer number of features it offers.

However, I've realized that I don't necessarily need all of those features to get around. For someone who primarily relies on walking directions, CoMaps gets the basics right, and its offline navigation alone makes it worth switching to. Add its privacy-focused approach, community-driven development, and growing support for reviews, and there's plenty to like.

You've probably heard people say that even if they've ditched most of Google's apps, there's one they just can't seem to give up: Google Maps. Interestingly, despite relying heavily on Google's ecosystem, from its Workspace apps to some of the experimental tools coming out of Google Labs, Google Maps was one app I barely ever opened.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

There were two reasons for that. I don't drive, and I don't live in a particularly walkable city. I rarely step out of the house to go somewhere I don't already know the directions to, and when I do, I'm usually with a friend who drives. But I've been traveling quite a bit lately, and Google Maps has gone from an app I'd rarely open to one of the most-used apps on my phone.

While I've grown to appreciate just how useful Google Maps is, I've also started wondering whether I really need to rely on Google to get around. So, I decided to put that to the test by replacing it with CoMaps, a completely free and open-source alternative.

CoMaps is a completely open-source alternative to Google Maps

A familiar app with a different philosophy

Now, this isn't my first time trying open-source Google Maps alternatives. I've been experimenting with them for a while now, and I even wrote about three alternatives I tested just a few days ago. One of the tools I covered was Organic Maps, a fairly well-known open-source Google Maps alternative. It's long been known for its privacy-focused approach and is built on OpenStreetMap data.

Interestingly, CoMaps is actually a fork of Organic Maps. It emerged in May 2025 following disagreements between Organic Maps' contributors and shareholders over the project's governance, financial transparency, and future direction. Several contributors ultimately decided to branch off and create CoMaps, a community-driven, not-for-profit alternative that prioritizes transparency and open-source development.

This means the two apps have a fair bit in common. Like Organic Maps, CoMaps prioritizes user privacy, doesn't require an account, and lets you download maps for offline navigation. It supports walking, cycling, and driving directions. It also doesn't bombard you with ads and is completely free from AI features you never asked for.

CoMaps takes its community-led approach seriously

A little help from the crowd goes a long way

CoMaps is built by its community for its community, and it seems to take this philosophy very seriously. Since it relies on OpenStreetMap data, users can contribute to the maps themselves, whether that's adding a missing business, correcting outdated opening hours, or updating information about an existing location. You can even make some of these changes directly through the app, although you'll need an OpenStreetMap account to do so.

While you can do all of the above with Organic Maps too, CoMaps takes things a step further with its integration with Mangrove Reviews. One of my biggest frustrations with the open-source alternatives I previously tested was the lack of ratings and reviews. After all, when you're exploring an unfamiliar city, knowing how to get somewhere is only half the battle. You also need to figure out whether that restaurant or café is actually worth visiting.

CoMaps attempts to address this with community-powered reviews. Since August 2026, Android users have been able to see star ratings and written reviews for places through Mangrove, an independent, open review platform. While you can technically access Mangrove reviews separately when using Organic Maps, CoMaps integrates them directly into the app, so you don't have to switch between services. Interestingly, these reviews are also downloaded alongside the maps, meaning you can access them even when you're offline. You can also contribute your own reviews through external tools like MapComplete.

There's a catch, though. Mangrove's database is still nowhere near as extensive as Google's. As of October 2026, it has just over 10,000 reviews worldwide, compared to the millions available on larger platforms. This means finding reviews for places near you can be a challenge. Still, it's an interesting step toward addressing one of the biggest advantages Google Maps has over its open-source competitors.

CoMaps has offline maps that actually work offline

Google Maps can't walk the walk

One of my biggest frustrations with Google Maps is just how limited its offline maps are. I mean, what good are offline maps if they can't actually give you the directions you need when you're offline? Plus, what's worse than discovering that limitation when you've already lost internet access?

I learned this the hard way when I was in Berlin for IFA. I needed to get a local SIM card from a store in the city center, which was closing in about an hour. I was alone in an unfamiliar city, had no mobile data, and needed to figure out how to get there as quickly as possible.

Now, you'd think having downloaded Google Maps' offline maps beforehand would've been enough. Unfortunately, that wasn't the case. While I could see the streets around me, Google Maps couldn't give me walking directions. With time running out, I ended up having to ask strangers for directions along the way.

The problem is that Google Maps only supports driving directions when you're offline. Walking, cycling, and public transit directions all require an internet connection. Given that I don't drive and spend most of my time walking whenever I'm traveling, this is a pretty major inconvenience.

This is where CoMaps makes a massive difference. Like Google Maps, you can download maps of entire regions beforehand. But unlike Google's offering, CoMaps lets you search for places, plan walking routes, and get turn-by-turn directions even when you're completely offline. You also get voice-guided navigation, and since GPS doesn't require an internet connection, you can still track your location without mobile data.

Essentially, instead of simply having a downloaded map that shows you where you are, you have an actual navigation app that can help you get to where you need to go.

The biggest thing I'm missing out on is live traffic data

Luckily, that's not my biggest concern

If there's one thing Google Maps is undeniably good at, it's live traffic data. Thanks to its massive user base, Google Maps can provide real-time traffic updates, identify congestion, and suggest alternative routes to help you avoid getting stuck in traffic. It's one of those features that can make a massive difference when you're trying to get somewhere on time.

Unfortunately, this is also one of the biggest things CoMaps lacks. It doesn't offer real-time traffic information, meaning you won't know whether a particular road is congested or if there's a faster route available. That said, this isn't much of a dealbreaker for me. I don't drive, and when I'm traveling, I'm almost always exploring on foot. So, while I can certainly see why the lack of live traffic data might be a major drawback for some people, it's not a feature I personally rely on very often.

I stopped using Android Auto's navigation and switched to offline maps, and now I never worry about signal loss

No signal, no problem

There's no confirmed timeline for when the feature will arrive, but it's reassuring to know that the developers are working on addressing this limitation.

For someone who primarily relies on walking directions, CoMaps gets the basics right, and its offline navigation alone makes it worth switching to. Add its privacy-focused approach, community-driven development, and growing support for reviews, and there's plenty to like.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With NVMe SSDs becoming the obvious choice when building or buying a new PC, and HDDs being the cheaper choice for mass storage, it's easy for SATA SSDs to fall between the cracks. You might think of them as the worst of both worlds, but they're far from worthless.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Recently, I threw out a 10-year-old laptop that had nothing left to give, but I did have a SATA SSD inside it that didn't get much use before I replaced the laptop, so I found a new purpose for that SSD. With a cheap enclosure, it became a perfect backup drive when I care about speed more than massive amounts of space.

This old SSD still has a lot of life in it

They last a long time

I'm not saying I would necessarily advise you to buy a new SATA SSD today, but there's a good chance that, like me, you have an old laptop lying around that could provide a nice backup drive if needed. It may sound like a bad idea to use a 10-year-old laptop's drive, but the drive itself is actually a good bit newer.

This laptop had originally shipped with an HDD, and it was only a couple of years later that I replaced that HDD with an SSD (that HDD also became a backup drive at the time), and then that laptop was superseded by another model not too long after, so it stopped being my most active device. All things considered, this SSD hasn't had a lot of writes on it, so it can still last me a good few years. I even decided to check with CrystalDiskInfo, and it reported the SSD health is at 94%, which is still pretty good.

And while SATA SSDs are nowhere near the speed of a modern NVMe SSD, they're still a good bit faster than an HDD, so moving data to and from them is going to take less time out of your day. It's not ideal if I want to back up large drives, but it's perfect for my needs because there's usually only a few gigabytes of data I need to back up at any given time, and this is just faster.

You don't need CrystalDiskInfo to check your SSD health, as Windows already tells you a lot

Most users don't need to know more than what Windows already tells you

1
By  Tanveer Singh

SATA enclosures are much cheaper

I could get one for under $20

In addition to the drives themselves, the ability to use them externally is also much cheaper compared to an NVMe drive. SATA SSDs typically come in a 2.5-inch form factor, and buying an enclosure for that size is dirt cheap. Mine cost me just under $20 and it offers USB 3.2 Gen 1 speeds, meaning I get 5Gbps of bandwidth. And you can find them even cheaper on websites like Amazon.

NVMe SSDs are certainly faster, but making use of that speed means you also need a faster USB protocol and more expensive hardware in the enclosure itself to handle the PCIe NVMe communication. You can find some cheaper options that use the same USB protocol, though they usually start at a little over $20, and even then, you'll be limiting yourself to USB 3.2 speeds, which are solid, but fall very short of what an NVMe drive can do.

Satechi Mini NVMe SSD enclosure review: An ultra-portable SSD housing for all your devices

This tiny SSD enclosure is the perfect pairing for your phone (or PC)

2
By  João Carrasqueira

If you want that NVMe drive to be worth its price, you need something like USB4 or Thunderbolt 4, and you won't find those enclosures for less than $60. That cost adds up, especially if we're comparing it to just reusing a drive you already have.

How does it compare to an HDD?

It's much faster... sometimes

Seeing as I have both an external HDD and an SSD at home, it's worth seeing how they compare in terms of speed. I should note that the HDD here is a fully enclosed and integrated solution, so I don't know the exact specs of the hard drive itself, but it does use USB 3.0, so the bus speed is the same.

I tried transferring the same set of files, totaling around 7GB, from my PC to the external drives, and then back to the PC using TeraCopy. Using the 1TB HDD, transferring the files from the PC took 1 minute and 16 seconds for an average speed of 94MB/s, while copying them back to the PC took 2 minutes and 3 seconds, averaging 58MB/s.

With the SSD, however, things are a little more complicated. This is a relatively low-end SSD and while it's much faster initially, speeds fall off a cliff after a couple of gigabytes have been written. With a 7GB transfer, copying files to the SSD actually ended up being a bit slower, at 1 minute and 46 seconds, averaging 64MB/s. Transferring the files back to the PC, however, took just 49 seconds, averaging 144MB/s.

My SSD hit a speed cliff after 19 seconds, and the spec sheet never warned me

Things got ugly past the advertised speeds

3
By  Samarveer Singh

It's worth looking at the speed graph above because, with the SSD, you can see write speeds start off much faster, nearing 400MB/s for the first 2GB transferred. If I'm backing up smaller files than 2GB, the SSD is nearly four times faster than the HDD, but it slows down the longer it goes on. As for read speeds, the SSD seems to spike up to nearly 400MB/s frequently during the transfer process, and in the end, the transfer was over twice as fast on average.

If I'm backing up things like photos, documents, or music on a regular basis, that 2GB limit is more than enough to make the SSD the fastest option by far. In some cases, though, the HDD will still win.

It's a great deal for the price

Considering I only had to spend under $20 to turns this SSD into a backup drive, I'd say those results are very positive. If I need mass storage, I might still back up files to my HDD, but if I need a quick backup, the SSD is easily the faster option, and it's faster to restore that data after I reset or format my PC, too. I'm glad I was careful to take out the SATA SSD before trashing my old laptop, because it can still come in handy often.

Storage Capacity
None included
Compatible Devices
2.5-inch SATA drives
Portable
Yes

This Sabrent SATA enclosure offers USB 3.0 speeds with a full-size USB Type-A port, and it's suitable for both HDDs and SSDs in a 2.5-inch form factor.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AI coding assistants have become capable, but I have always felt that there is a catch. Whether I am using Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, I often end up working within a particular ecosystem.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That’s why OpenCode immediately caught my attention. It’s a free, open-source AI coding agent that promises something different: the freedom to choose my preferred AI models, work across different environments, and even run everything locally for greater privacy.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

What is OpenCode, and why did I try it?

An open-source challenger worth exploring

OpenCode is a free, open-source AI coding agent. At first glance, it may look like another Claude Code alternative, but there is more to it than that. Unlike coding assistants tied to a particular AI provider, OpenCode lets you choose the models you want to work with.

Having experimented extensively with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, I wanted to explore something that offered more freedom without compromising essential coding capabilities. I especially liked the idea of switching between AI models by task instead of relying on a single provider.

The possibility of running coding agents locally for better privacy was another major reason I decided to give OpenCode a shot.

I am no longer tied to one AI provider

One interface, dozens of AI models

One of my biggest frustrations with AI coding assistants is how easily I end up depending on a particular AI provider. With Claude Code, I am mainly working with Anthropic’s ecosystem, while Codex revolves around OpenAI’s models. Similarly, Cursor focuses on Grok models by default.

In comparison, OpenCode supports more than 75 AI providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, and OpenRouter. For example, I could use Claude for complex reasoning, Gemini for everyday development, and a different model for debugging or smaller coding tasks.

I can finally keep my code private

Local AI changes the privacy equation

Privacy is another major reason I find OpenCode so appealing. Most mainstream AI coding assistants rely heavily on cloud-based models, which means portions of my codebase and prompts may be sent to external servers for processing.

OpenCode gives me another option. I can connect it to Ollama, run a compatible coding model locally, and handle development tasks without sending my source code to an external AI provider.

OpenCode has also helped me rethink how I spend my AI coding budget. I don’t necessarily need a premium Claude model for every little task. For straightforward jobs like generating boilerplate code, tweaking CSS, creating basic components, or fixing minor bugs, I prefer using the capable free models like DeepSeek or Beam through OpenCode.

This approach lets me reserve my Claude Code usage and tokens for projects that genuinely demand stronger reasoning, complex debugging, architectural decisions, or codebase refactoring.

I tried creating a complex website using the space-bunny-free model, and it did a solid job at first glance. Of course, free cloud models don’t offer the same privacy benefits as running AI locally, and smaller local models may struggle with demanding projects. Still, I appreciate having these choices within a single application.

I asked Claude Code to build its own replacement, and it took just 15 minutes

15 minutes and one crazy idea later...

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I can work from almost anywhere

Open-source changes the cost equation

Another thing I appreciate is its flexibility across development environments. OpenCode offers a terminal-based interface, a dedicated desktop app, and IDE integration. Whether you prefer working directly from the command line or using a more familiar graphical interface, there is an option available.

Since I frequently switch between my Windows desktop and MacBook, having a consistent coding assistant across both platforms is a huge convenience.

For example, I can start building a personal finance dashboard using OpenCode on my Windows PC and later continue working on the same project from my MacBook after syncing the project files. I can also launch OpenCode from VS Code without leaving my existing workflow.

The dedicated desktop interface is useful when I don’t feel like dealing with terminal commands.

This flexibility may sound like a small convenience, but it makes OpenCode much easier to incorporate into my everyday development routine. I get the power of a terminal-based AI agent without being restricted to the terminal.

OpenCode’s open-source nature is another major advantage. I don’t need another expensive monthly subscription just to access the coding agent. Better yet, I can connect several capable free AI models for routine development tasks.

For instance, if I need to adjust a dashboard’s CSS, generate a simple component, or fix a minor JavaScript error, I can use a free model instead of consuming my premium Claude Code allowance.

A smarter alternative to closed ecosystems

It’s easy to get comfortable with a coding assistant that works well and never bother looking elsewhere. However, experimenting with OpenCode has reminded me why it’s important to keep exploring alternatives.

Between its open-source nature, support for multiple AI providers, local model integration, and powerful customization options, there is plenty to appreciate here.

So, what are you waiting for? Keep experimenting, challenge your existing workflow, and give alternatives like OpenCode a fair chance.

OpenCode

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That’s why OpenCode immediately caught my attention. It’s a free, open-source AI coding agent that promises something different: the freedom to choose my preferred AI models, work across different environments, and even run everything locally for greater privacy.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

What is OpenCode, and why did I try it?

An open-source challenger worth exploring

OpenCode is a free, open-source AI coding agent. At first glance, it may look like another Claude Code alternative, but there is more to it than that. Unlike coding assistants tied to a particular AI provider, OpenCode lets you choose the models you want to work with.

Having experimented extensively with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, I wanted to explore something that offered more freedom without compromising essential coding capabilities. I especially liked the idea of switching between AI models by task instead of relying on a single provider.

The possibility of running coding agents locally for better privacy was another major reason I decided to give OpenCode a shot.

I am no longer tied to one AI provider

One interface, dozens of AI models

One of my biggest frustrations with AI coding assistants is how easily I end up depending on a particular AI provider. With Claude Code, I am mainly working with Anthropic’s ecosystem, while Codex revolves around OpenAI’s models. Similarly, Cursor focuses on Grok models by default.

In comparison, OpenCode supports more than 75 AI providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, and OpenRouter. For example, I could use Claude for complex reasoning, Gemini for everyday development, and a different model for debugging or smaller coding tasks.

I can finally keep my code private

Local AI changes the privacy equation

Privacy is another major reason I find OpenCode so appealing. Most mainstream AI coding assistants rely heavily on cloud-based models, which means portions of my codebase and prompts may be sent to external servers for processing.

OpenCode gives me another option. I can connect it to Ollama, run a compatible coding model locally, and handle development tasks without sending my source code to an external AI provider.

OpenCode has also helped me rethink how I spend my AI coding budget. I don’t necessarily need a premium Claude model for every little task. For straightforward jobs like generating boilerplate code, tweaking CSS, creating basic components, or fixing minor bugs, I prefer using the capable free models like DeepSeek or Beam through OpenCode.

This approach lets me reserve my Claude Code usage and tokens for projects that genuinely demand stronger reasoning, complex debugging, architectural decisions, or codebase refactoring.

I tried creating a complex website using the space-bunny-free model, and it did a solid job at first glance. Of course, free cloud models don’t offer the same privacy benefits as running AI locally, and smaller local models may struggle with demanding projects. Still, I appreciate having these choices within a single application.

I asked Claude Code to build its own replacement, and it took just 15 minutes

15 minutes and one crazy idea later...

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I can work from almost anywhere

Open-source changes the cost equation

Another thing I appreciate is its flexibility across development environments. OpenCode offers a terminal-based interface, a dedicated desktop app, and IDE integration. Whether you prefer working directly from the command line or using a more familiar graphical interface, there is an option available.

Since I frequently switch between my Windows desktop and MacBook, having a consistent coding assistant across both platforms is a huge convenience.

For example, I can start building a personal finance dashboard using OpenCode on my Windows PC and later continue working on the same project from my MacBook after syncing the project files. I can also launch OpenCode from VS Code without leaving my existing workflow.

The dedicated desktop interface is useful when I don’t feel like dealing with terminal commands.

This flexibility may sound like a small convenience, but it makes OpenCode much easier to incorporate into my everyday development routine. I get the power of a terminal-based AI agent without being restricted to the terminal.

OpenCode’s open-source nature is another major advantage. I don’t need another expensive monthly subscription just to access the coding agent. Better yet, I can connect several capable free AI models for routine development tasks.

For instance, if I need to adjust a dashboard’s CSS, generate a simple component, or fix a minor JavaScript error, I can use a free model instead of consuming my premium Claude Code allowance.

A smarter alternative to closed ecosystems

It’s easy to get comfortable with a coding assistant that works well and never bother looking elsewhere. However, experimenting with OpenCode has reminded me why it’s important to keep exploring alternatives.

Between its open-source nature, support for multiple AI providers, local model integration, and powerful customization options, there is plenty to appreciate here.

So, what are you waiting for? Keep experimenting, challenge your existing workflow, and give alternatives like OpenCode a fair chance.

OpenCode

OpenCode is an open-source alternative to Claude Code and Codex.

item.title: KDE Plasma gets a ton of bug fixes as 6.8 begins landing on people's computers
item.itunes:title: KDE Plasma gets a ton of bug fixes as 6.8 begins landing on people's computers
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Plasma 6.8 shipped on October 14, meaning daily drivers are now finding bugs that dodged beta testers.
  • Community fixed regressions like wrong notification placement and cloned panel screen bugs.
  • 6.8.2 fixed Discover crashes and Flatpak remote desktop crashes; some fixes move to 6.9.

So, how's everyone liking KDE Plasma 6.8? It was released on October 14th, which means people who aren't on LTS branches have likely gotten it already. Unfortunately, as is always the case, some bugs managed to sneak in, because nothing stress-tests a desktop environment like shipping it out to daily drivers across the world.

Fortunately, the KDE community has been hard at work squashing every bug they see, and we've got a fresh batch of fixes. So, if something has been bugging you with the new build, it's worth taking a look to see if it got fixed in a recent update.

KDE Plasma saw a ton of bug fixes this week as the team settles down after 6.8

The community is making excellent progress

As covered in KDE's official This Week in Plasma blog, the community has been tackling all the regressions that happened with 6.8. Regressions happen when features that used to work fine break after an update, so it's important to fix them before anything else happens.

Reported regressions included notifications popping up at the top-left when you didn't ask them to appear there, an annoying bug where cloned panels would forget which screen they were set on, and a bug that caused Plasma to fall over if you had over a total of 16 screens, virtual desktops, and/or activities, then opened the launcher widget with a keyboard shortcut.

Once the regressions were sorted, the KDE community could start fixing more long-standing bugs. Plasma 6.8.2 fixed three different ways Discover could crash while updating your system with it, and also fixed a bug that would cause a remote desktop session to crash if you launched it from within a Flatpak. Some issues were moved to 6.9's release, such as hitting a "Full Screen" button on a website in the Web Browser widget actually going into full-screen mode, which definitely sounds useful.

As such, if 6.8 broke some of your favorite features, now would be a good time to give your desktop environment an update and see if your problem got fixed.

After years of bugs, KDE Plasma 6.8 is turning on triple buffering for NVIDIA GPUs by default

Gaming on Linux is about to get a little bit better.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: Sam Altman says it's "quite terrible" that people use RAM in their PCs for AI during a shortage
item.itunes:title: Sam Altman says it's "quite terrible" that people use RAM in their PCs for AI during a shortage
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AI demand is driving up RAM costs, making consumer sticks pricier.
  • Altman implies underused PC RAM should be in cloud data centers for higher utilization in an interview.
  • His remarks suggest a preference for cloud over consumer RAM, which shows a worrying trend if true.

If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to. Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs. Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs.

People using the RAM in their PCs 5% of the time is "quite terrible," says OpenAI's Sam Altman

It was from a "global allocation perspective," but it's still a worrying one

Over in an interview on the Cheeky Pint (via IGN), Sam Altman discussed the current state of RAM. In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware. However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing:

From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and being used maybe 5% of the time. Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that.

It seems his point was that, in a shortage, he would prefer RAM in data centers where it'll be put to task for hours in a day, rather than someone's computer where it'll only be used a fraction of the time. And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means.

But overall, I feel his statement has partially shown his hand and disposition toward consumers, particularly the last sentence: "And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." I got the feeling that he thinks RAM sticks in his data centers are worth more than the RAM in people's PCs, whether they run AI off them or not. As if people should allow OpenAI to have the lion's share of RAM so that it can run more powerful AI models in the cloud. And that really comes off poorly in my eyes.

Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage. However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit.

The 16GB gaming PC is officially dead and current RAM pricing proves it

32GB has become the new minimum and my testing proved it for me.

15
By  Jasmine Mannan

item.title: Epic's Linux anti-cheat wants TPM 2.0 and a stack of settings, and you can check your own PC in about five minutes
item.itunes:title: Epic's Linux anti-cheat wants TPM 2.0 and a stack of settings, and you can check your own PC in about five minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Windows 11 arrived on the block, people running Windows 10 with older hardware hit a brick wall. Windows 11 requires a CPU with TPM 2.0, and if yours didn't have it, you had to perform workarounds just to get it installed. The alternative was to move to Linux, where TPM 1.2 chips were supported, and still are.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, it appears even Linux isn't totally free from TPM shenanigans. If you love competitive gaming, Epic Games' Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) version 2 will require you to have a TPM 2.0 chip to play its games.

Epic Games' Easy Anti-Cheat didn't play nicely with Linux at all...

It was causing some real issues for Linux gamers

Before we hop into what EAC v2 brings, we have to take a look at the first version. EAC is a kernel-level anti-cheat that Epic Games uses to ensure people don't cheat in its popular online games, like Fortnite. Deploying kernel-level anti-cheat is just fine when the kernel in question is locked down and proprietary, like Windows'. It's not so great when using it on an OS where the kernel is open-source, and anyone can tinker with it, like Linux's.

EAC’s relationship with Linux has been pretty rough. Epic didn't completely ignore it; after all, we saw native support arrive in 2014, and Proton/Wine compatibility in 2021. But because these ran in the user space and weren't locked-down kernel drivers, Epic made them optional.

Unsurprisingly, most developers took the simplest route to prevent Linux-based cheaters: saying no to Linux entirely. When you're trying to run a competitive multiplayer online game, ruining its reputation just so a smattering of players on CachyOS can play is more trouble than it's worth, which is why even Epic kept Fortnite off Linux. Well, the good news is, Epic Games found a way to include Linux, but people with older hardware won't be too fond of it.

I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting

If I can't completely escape Windows, I can just offload it onto something else

4
By  Ty Sherback

...but v2 will allow some Linux gamers in if they have the hardware

Better than nothing, I suppose

On October 14th, Epic Games posted a blog detailing its plans for Linux. It'll release what it calls EAC Linux v2, and the objective is to bring "the level of protection much closer to par with Windows, in the very near term." To do this, it will use existing Linux features to get the job done.

While it won't use a kernel module like Windows, it will need a laundry list of hardware. For starters, you need to be using a distro with a signed kernel. Your PC needs Secure Boot enabled, and your boot loader needs to have Measured Boot. You also need IOMMU, Kernel Lockdown Integrity Mode, and the Linux Security Module BPF all enabled, and Kexec, a feature that lets you load a new kernel without rebooting, must be disabled.

However, one entry on the list will bring back bad Windows 11 memories:

TPM 2.0 is standard on modern consumer hardware, and software support is built into the Linux kernel. We require that systems have TPM 2.0 support and that it is enabled in the BIOS.

Epic Games cites TPM 2.0's technologies like Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) as the reason why it's demanding it, claiming it allows for a "tamper-resistant boot log to be produced and verified." This should allow EAC Linux v2 to look at what code ran during boot without needing to actually run at boot. However, it does mean that TPM 1.2 users are left behind.

There is some good news, such as EAC Linux v2 being a systemd service that only loads when a protected game boots up and closes when it's finished. But it's not ideal for anyone who uses Linux because of its older hardware compatibility. One could argue that someone with a PC that fails these tests probably isn't playing competitive games anyway, but it is confirmed in the blog post's FAQ section that the Steam Deck is still left high and dry for compatibility.

Linux is now adopting a CPU requirement Windows already demands, but don't worry, it's not TPM 2.0

In fact, if you're reading this line, your computer's CPU is most definitely still supported.

7
By  Simon Batt

Giving your Linux a quick check-up is simple

You just need to run a few commands

To see whether your Linux PC fits the bill, run these quick commands. They'll let you know if your PC passes at least five of the eight requirements:

  • Secure Boot: mokutil --sb-state should say it's enabled.
  • TPM 2.0: cat /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major reporting a "2" means you have TPM 2.0. A "1" means you're on TPM 1.2.
  • Kernel Lockdown: cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown must show [integrity]for it to be valid.
  • BPF LSM: cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm must include bpfto prove compatibility.
  • Kexec: cat /proc/sys/kernel/kexec_load_disabled must output 1.
Nvidia’s RTX Spark passed most of my anti-cheat tests, but Valorant and Call of Duty still won’t run (yet)

Anti-cheat support from Riot Games, CoD, and EA are in the works

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Gaming on Linux is getting easier, for some

All things considered, I'm grateful Epic Games is doing something to allow more Linux gamers to play online. I just wish it didn't have to include the shadow of Windows 11's system requirements.

item.title: I stopped paying for Lightroom after finding a free open-source editor that handles my RAW files just as well
item.itunes:title: I stopped paying for Lightroom after finding a free open-source editor that handles my RAW files just as well
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The industry standard for working with RAW files has been Adobe Lightroom for nearly two decades, but being tied down to a subscription has left myself and many other users with a bad taste in our mouths. Paying every month for software I mostly use for product shots has always felt like renting a screwdriver, and the free alternatives all had their own unique workflow that I didn't want to adopt in full.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

LightCraft is the first one I've come across that doesn't force me to change my workflow but also has most of the features I use daily. It's very young and was made with some heavy assistance from Claude Opus, so there are some places where it doesn't match Adobe, but for the way I shoot, it's the perfect replacement.

An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing

ArtCraft has seriously impressed me

6
By  Ty Sherback

It feels like Lightroom, which is so important

I'm not re-learning how to import and edit photos with LightCraft

I primarily shoot product shots on my iPhone 18 Pro, but on occasion, I do shoot on a Rebel T3i, which give me 14-bit CR2 files. These are a very common older format that could trip up a newer piece of software if it's not configured correctly, but LightCraft imports them easily, and has supported them from its earliest working build. The project has since checked decoded CR2 files from a long list of Canon bodies against each one's own JPEG, so it's got pretty good support for them.

The file import process is very similar to Lightroom, and once the files are in, editing them feels very natural. Exposure, white balance, tone curves, masking, cropping and upright perspective correction sit roughly where a Lightroom user would expect them, and every change made to the photo is stored as an edit rather than written into the original file. Presets, version history and copying settings across a batch also work the way they do in Lightroom.

RapidRAW is the free, open-source Lightroom alternative I've been waiting for

Editing photos is about to get a whole lot easier

8
By  João Carrasqueira

It ditches the parts of Lightroom that make Adobe apps a pain

No subscription, compatibility with Linux, and completely open-source

I think the thing that has me truly hooked onto LightCraft is the bits that aren't technical, though. Lightroom's primary lock-in is years of habit, and thankfully, LightCraft doesn't make any statements with its design or UI. It's trying to be 1:1 for the stuff you'll use in the app, and it ditches most of the annoying things that make Adobe apps painful to use.

LightCraft is completely free and open-source, which is huge for an app that feels so close to a first-party Adobe app. Everything runs locally on Windows, macOS, and even Linux, which is a bonus for someone like me who doesn't want to constantly switch devices from the Linux machine I'm writing on to edit photos. It's also really fast to boot up and feels snappy to click around in—I didn't notice any slowdowns while editing or scrolling through my library.

6 reasons Darktable is better than Adobe Lightroom for hobbyist photo editors

Why pay for Lightroom when Darktable does more?

7
By  Nolen Jonker

Where it still falls short of Adobe Lightroom

LightCraft won't be a complete replacement for many

Color is by far the biggest gap between LightCraft and Lightroom, and it's not particularly close. Adobe ships tuned profiles for an enormous range of cameras, including Camera Matching profiles that mimic each body’s in-camera looks. LightCraft can’t use those. It relies on data stored in DNG files, its own fitted profiles for a handful of cameras, and look estimates built from camera JPEGs for certain formats. Older CR2 files like mine aren’t on that list, so they start from a more neutral rendering.

Lens correction is another place where it falls behind a bit. Lightroom matches thousands of lens profiles automatically, while LightCraft only applies the corrections that the camera wrote into the file itself. My camera doesn't produce a format it can read those from, so things like distortion and vignetting on my kit lens are manual adjustments I have to make.

AI features like masking and denoise are still in progress, but there is the ability to load a local model to perform some actions within LightCraft. Subject and sky selection use more traditional detection rather than an AI model, while object selection and AI denoise both depend on optional local models you install yourself. AI Denoise also only works on traditional Bayer-sensor RAW files for now, so it won’t touch my iPhone’s ProRAW shots. I haven’t tested how well the local tools perform myself.

I tried replacing Photoshop, Lightroom, and Acrobat with free vibe-coded alternatives, and they're surprisingly good

Got to give credit where credit's due

10
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Where familiar still beats the mature options

Lightroom refugees that perform the simple edits will be at home

Credit: 

Friction is such a large part of why LightCraft exists in the first place, and I think eliminating it is naturally going to pull a lot of users off of Lightroom and other FOSS options, even if it's not totally feature complete. For the average person editing some photos that their iPhone took in ProRAW or their older DSLR, the features are already there. The professional photographer will still need what Adobe offers, at least right now. And for them, the monthly investment in the software is absolutely worthwhile. Things like gaps in color profiles and lack of support for some formats just means it will be unusable for those kinds of users, but for the weekend photographer like me, it's perfect.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Should you cancel your Adobe subscription?

Whether you should actually cancel your subscription depends on what camera you shoot with and what you actually use Lightroom for. If your body is well-supported, your edits are mostly global adjustments and presets, and you’re comfortable doing lens corrections by hand, LightCraft is already a credible free replacement, with seemingly more features on the way. If you depend on Adobe’s camera profiles, automatic lens corrections, AI denoise or mobile sync, I'd keep paying for now.

item.title: I gave ChatGPT Dots access to my email, calendar, and tasks, and it started helping without being asked
item.itunes:title: I gave ChatGPT Dots access to my email, calendar, and tasks, and it started helping without being asked
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Right now, the AI trend every company seems to be jumping on are always-on AI assistants that don't just wait around for you to give them instructions. OpenClaw helped kick off the craze for always-on AI assistants earlier this year. It wasn't long before major AI companies began experimenting with their own takes on the concept. Anthropic introduced Claude Dispatch, Meta launched Muse, and OpenAI eventually joined the party with ChatGPT Dots at its DevDay conference in September.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've been testing Dots for the last two weeks or so, and I've taken the bold step of connecting it to a bunch of tools I rely on daily. Turns out, the promise of having an AI assistant that proactively helps you without being asked isn't as far-fetched as I initially thought.

So, what even are ChatGPT Dots?

Think ChatGPT, but with a mind of its own

OpenAI describes Dots as always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. Think of them as personal AI assistants that don't just sit around waiting for you to give them instructions. Instead, they can proactively look for ways to help you, keep track of ongoing tasks, and even get work done without you having to ask.

Dots can connect to the apps and services you already rely on through OpenAI's ecosystem of plugins. Once connected, they can keep an eye on what's happening across these apps, flag things that might need your attention, and help you stay on top of your responsibilities. They also learn your preferences over time, so ideally, the longer you work with your Dot, the better it gets at understanding what matters to you.

Note: Dots are currently limited to select paid plans, including ChatGPT Pro, which starts at a whopping $100 per month! OpenAI provided me with complimentary access to ChatGPT Pro to test the feature, but had no editorial input or influence over this article. All opinions expressed are my own.

Each Dot also gets its own cloud computer and browser, which means it can take on more complicated tasks without relying on your own device. You can assign it multiple projects, let it work on them simultaneously, and even close ChatGPT entirely while it continues working in the background. You can also view its computer to see what it's doing, or take over the controls yourself when needed.

Getting Dots connected to my digital life was surprisingly easy

A few clicks later, I had a personal assistant

The concept behind OpenClaw was so well-received for a good reason. Beyond the privacy concerns, though, one of its biggest drawbacks, especially when it first went viral, was the technical barrier to getting started. You needed to be comfortable running terminal commands, configuring AI models, and setting up integrations before you could really start using it.

Sure, none of this was necessarily impossible for someone with a technical background, but it wasn't exactly the kind of tool an average person could just open and start using, either. Dots eliminates much of this friction. If you're comfortable using ChatGPT for your everyday tasks, you can set up a Dot and begin using it. I'd argue that it's even simpler than that!

ChatGPT essentially walks you through the entire process. You give your Dot a name, customize its appearance, and choose which apps and services you want it to access. I connected mine to Gmail, Google Calendar, Asana, Slack, Notion, Outlook, and a few other tools I rely on daily.

The entire process took just a few minutes, and there were no terminal commands, API keys, or complicated configurations to worry about.

What I particularly like is how approachable OpenAI has made the entire experience. From the adorable little characters you can customize to the fact that interacting with your Dot feels just like having a regular ChatGPT conversation, there's very little about it that feels intimidating.

Dots started helping before I even asked

Dots understood the assignment before I gave it one

One of the biggest selling points of Dots is that they don't necessarily need you to tell them what to do. They're designed to proactively look for ways to help, and while I was initially a little skeptical about how useful that would actually be, it turned out to be one of my favorite things about the entire experience.

$900 at Best Buy

All the power you need on the go

The Legion Go S 8 powered by SteamOS features some impressive hardware to run all your favorite games. You get a AMD Ryzen Z1 Extreme chip paired with 32GB of RAM and 1TB of SSD storage. There's also a microSD card slot if you want to add extra storage, with support for up to 2TB.
